speaker: Doctor
text: Can you tell me exactly how long this lesion has been present and whether you've noticed any fever or fatigue?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. She recalls an ant bite at the site before the lesion developed. She has a history of anterior uveitis treated with corticosteroids 8 months ago, as well as Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Given your history of Crohn's disease and diabetes, I need to know if the ulcer has a "punched-out" appearance with undermined borders, and are there any signs of infection like purulent drainage or spreading redness? Please also tell me if you have any visual changes or new abdominal pain.

REQUEST TEST: CBC, ESR, CRP; REQUEST IMAGES: Photograph of the leg lesion.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Skin Examination - Inspection reveals a 4-cm tender ulcerative lesion on the anterior right leg with a central necrotic base and purplish irregular borders; pitting pedal edema and dilated tortuous veins are noted. Palpation shows tenderness over the lesion with palpable femoral and pedal pulses bilaterally. Blood_Glucose_Level (Random) is Elevated. Complete_Blood_Count shows Normal WBC, Hemoglobin, and Platelets. Skin_Biopsy Histopathology shows neutrophilic infiltration without infection, consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum. Vital_Signs: Temperature 37.6°C, Pulse 98/min, Blood_Pressure 126/88 mm Hg.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Pyoderma Gangrenosum. This is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis often associated with your history of Crohn's disease and diabetes, triggered by minor trauma like the reported ant bite. The biopsy findings of neutrophilic infiltration without infection confirm the diagnosis. I will initiate treatment with systemic corticosteroids and coordinate with your gastroenterology team to optimize your Crohn's management.
